source.title: AutoInterpretation Finds Sparse Coding Beats Alternatives

record.file_problem: none; the full post text is present, but the referenced figures are not rendered with readable numerical values.
record.tranche_reason: It uses a different measurement procedure from the pole audit: GPT-4-generated explanations are scored by GPT-3.5 predictions on held-out fragments, including a comparison of top-and-random scores with separate top-only and random-only scores. It reports that explanations fail to account for within-fragment variation in residual-stream activations.
record.gate_note: The post evaluates sparse-coding features against neuron-basis and other dictionaries, but does not test the Qwen3-32B pole-job proportions, the cross-model/scale proportions, InceptionV1 examples, or neuron-based attribution graphs. The charts are referenced but their numerical means and confidence intervals are not present in the supplied text. The MLP comparison and other dictionary baselines are not direct tests of the listed claim versions; the post’s explicit residual-stream finding about failure to explain activation variation is relevant to V6.
record.test_reason: The post uses OpenAI's automated explanation-and-simulation scoring as a tool to rank its own sparse-coding dictionaries against baselines in Pythia70M. Neuron-basis scores appear only as an unreadable baseline in figures. It gives no share of neurons with good scores (V7) and no audit of neuron jobs (V1, V2). Its within-fragment finding concerns residual-stream directions, which are not neurons, and mostly the learned features. So the post does not test any version as stated. Its findings fit related constructs only.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find sparse coding beats all tested baselines in the MLP and, on separated top-only and random-only scores, in the residual stream. They warn that the combined score misleads for fragment-wide residual features. They also read the results as evidence that networks use distributed linear features only weakly anchored to the neuron basis, which the record's paraphrase omits.
record.recipe_differences: Uses OpenAI’s automatic-interpretation procedure to compare learned feature dictionaries and neuron-basis features, rather than auditing neuron poles and estimating their job counts.
record.method_sensitivity: The residual-stream conclusion changes with the scoring aggregation: sparse-coding features do not exceed the neuron basis on the combined top-and-random score, but outperform baselines on the separated top-only and random-only scores.

fits_no_version.finding: In the Pythia70M layer-2 residual stream, GPT-4 explanations from top fragments separate high-activation fragments from random ones but do not explain within-fragment variation. This inflates the combined top-and-random correlation, including for residual basis directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Top-and-random simulation scores can overstate explanation quality for directions with fragment-wide persistent activation; within-fragment correlation can be near zero.

fits_no_version.finding: In the MLP (layer 1), sparse-coding dictionary features get higher automated interpretability scores than the neuron basis and random directions. The advantage holds without the bias. PCA and ICA directions do not beat the neuron basis.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learned sparse dictionary directions are more interpretable by automated scoring than individual MLP neurons in a small LM.

record.problems: The authors describe the results as preliminary. Only 40–150 features per dictionary were interpreted; the MLP dictionary was the first and only MLP sparse-coding dictionary tested this way. The supplied text does not give readable numerical chart values, and the residual-stream method used tied encoder and decoder weights, with the difference left for future work.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows. Numerical means and confidence intervals in Figures 1–6 could not be transcribed because the supplied text contains only figure references and captions.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B pole audit or job shares.
No cross-model or scale shares; only Pythia70M.
No test of architecture, regularization or tools raising the share of interpretable neurons.
No attribution graphs or reconstruction error.
No test of whether neuron explanations drawn from activating examples fail to predict firing. The analogous finding concerns residual-stream directions.
Neuron-basis automated scores exist only in figures, with no threshold or share of well-scored neurons reported.

missing.what: Mean automated-interpretation scores and 95% confidence intervals for MLP neuron-basis directions, for top-and-random, top-only and random-only scoring. These would be needed to compare with V7's minority-of-good-scores claim, but they appear only in the figures.

record.verdict_notes: Preliminary results on 40–150 features per dictionary, from one model (Pythia70M). The post's framing (features weakly anchored to neurons) runs against the essay's spirit, but it reports no neuron-share numbers to test any version.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit or proportions of neuron poles assigned one job, two jobs, or not understood.
No comparison of interpretability shares across language models, model sizes, dense models, or mixture-of-experts models.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example or analysis of recursive generalization versus superposition.
No InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates or test of architecture, regularization, or tool quality changing the share of interpretable neurons.
No attribution graphs or reconstruction-error comparison.
Tests automatic explanations on Pythia70M activations and reports a residual-stream result; it does not test other models or quantify how often neuron explanations fail.
Although it runs automatic interpretation scoring, it does not report the fraction of neuron explanations above a stated good-score threshold or establish that only a minority meet such a threshold.

rows.subject: Pythia70M
rows.operation_detail: Compared automatic-interpretation scores for sparse-coding features with dictionary baselines.
rows.measure: Mean correlation between simulated and true feature activations
rows.value: Sparse-coding features outperform both the neuron basis and random directions; numerical scores are figure only.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals around means are shown in the figure; values not readable in supplied text.
rows.note: The post also reports that PCA and ICA directions do not outperform the neuron basis; the first approximately 30 PCA components tend to be highly interpretable, with later components not noticeably outperforming it.
rows.check: This compares the study's own sparse-coding dictionary with the MLP neuron basis. It is the study's method against baselines, not a measure of any version. The neuron-basis score is not readable (figure only), so it cannot speak to V7's minority-of-good-scores claim.

rows.subject: Pythia70M
rows.operation_detail: Scored explanations generated from highly activating fragments using simulated activations on top and random fragments.
rows.measure: Correlation between simulated and true activations
rows.baseline: Neuron-basis features; numerical baseline not stated
rows.value: Sparse-coding mean score is no higher than the neuron-basis mean; numerical scores are figure only.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals around means are shown in the figure; values not readable in supplied text.
rows.note: The post calls this a null result for the combined top-and-random measure and says the measure can be misleading.
rows.check: Linked to V6 in error. The row compares sparse-coding features with residual-stream basis directions on the combined score, and the authors say sparse coding is no better. That is a method comparison, not V6's failure of neuron explanations to predict firing. The state should read absent (no advantage), not partial.

rows.measure: Correlation between simulated and true activations
rows.baseline: Neuron-basis and other tested dictionary features
rows.value: Learned sparse-coding features outperform all tested baselines; numerical scores are figure only.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals around means are shown in the figure; values not readable in supplied text.
rows.note: The post reports this separately from the combined top-and-random score.
rows.check: This is the study's own method beating baselines on top-only fragments. It is not a V6 measure.

rows.measure: Correlation between simulated and true activations
rows.baseline: Neuron-basis and other tested dictionary features
rows.value: Learned sparse-coding features outperform all tested baselines; numerical scores are figure only.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals around means are shown in the figure; values not readable in supplied text.
rows.note: The post says the combined measure does not show this advantage, whereas the separated scores do.

rows.subject: Pythia70M
rows.operation_detail: Compared explanation-predicted activations with true activations within residual-stream text fragments.

conditions.value: highly activating fragments, including number-heavy text

rows.measure: Ability of explanations to account for activation variation within a fragment
rows.value: Explanations distinguish broadly high-scoring fragments from random fragments but do not explain the activation variation within the fragments.
rows.locator: Residual Stream Results; discussion following Figures 5–6
rows.note: Explanations were generated from highly activating fragments and then simulated on separate fragments; the post attributes the weak combined correlation to persistent, fragment-wide activation and unexplained within-fragment variation.
rows.check: The subject is residual-stream directions (basis and learned), not neurons. The residual stream has no privileged neuron basis. The finding is that explanations match fragment-level on/off but not within-fragment variation. That resembles V6's concern but is about a different unit, and the post gives no rate. It belongs under fits_no_version.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The post explicitly reports that generated explanations capture broad differences between fragments but fail to explain variation within them (r5); the separated fragment scores alongside the combined-score result show why a score can obscure this failure (r2–r4).
